label: bm-simulation-fem
topic: An open, runnable simulation of the bilayer that checks the law
summary: I built and ran, in Python with numpy, scipy and scikit-fem 12.0.2 (all installed on D:), four independent models of a two-layer strip with differential swelling: (1) a 1-D force and moment balance solved by linear algebra, (2) a 2-D finite-element model in plane stress and plane strain, (3) a 3-D linear finite-element model for finite widths, and (4) a large-deflection (von Karman) Rayleigh-Ritz plate model. Result 1: the project-record Timoshenko coefficient f(m,n) is reproduced by the 1-D balance to 2.9e-15 and by the 2-D plane-stress FEM to a maximum relative error of 1.2e-7 (worst point n=10, m=0.05) over n=1,2,5,10,50 and m=0.05..20; the FEM maximum is 1.50000 at m=n^-0.5 for every n, so the 3/2 ceiling and the 'modulus ratio drops out' statement are confirmed numerically, and extended to a 2000:1 stiffness contrast (error under 2e-4 off-optimum, 5e-5 at the optimum). Result 2 (new, qualifies the ceiling): the 3/2 ceiling holds for a free strip (plane stress). If the strip is so wide that it is held to a cylinder (plane strain, no cross-curl) the coefficient becomes (1+nu1) f, where nu1 is the Poisson ratio of the swelling layer: ceiling 1.95 for nu=0.30 (+30 percent) and 2.235 for nu=0.49 (+49 percent); the modulus ratio still drops out. With different Poisson ratios in the two layers (0.49 and 0.35) the plane-strain curvature is between 1.29 and 1.67 times the plain Timoshenko value over the grid. Result 3: with 3-D linear FEM, equal Poisson ratios and any width from 1 to 32 thicknesses (length 20 thicknesses), the curvature along the strip equals Timoshenko to better than 1e-4; with Poisson ratios 0.49 (swelling layer) and 0.35 (passive layer) it is 0.3 percent low at worst; and the cross-width curvature is synclastic (same sign, ratio +1.000 for widths of 4 thicknesses or more), not anticlastic, because swelling is an isotropic free strain, not an applied moment. Result 4: the real width effect is geometric. In the von Karman Ritz model (length 40 thicknesses) the curvature along the strip falls below Timoshenko by 1.4 percent when f*d_eps*(w/h)^2 = 0.96, by 5.8 percent at 2.2, by 13 percent at 3.8 and by 27 percent at 8.6 (optimum n=10 bilayer, 1 percent swelling); this puts numbers on the earlier sqrt(h/kappa) scale. The sphere-to-cylinder switch is gradual in this model and the cylinder amplification (1+nu) was not reached inside the range where the model is valid. Design consequence (inputs from the project record, flagged as estimates): a soft Flexible-80A-like layer over a Rigid-10K-like layer is a stiffness contrast near 1800:1, whose 3/2 optimum needs the stiff layer to be 2.3 percent of the thickness; at the 0.2 mm Form 4 minimum supported wall that is a 8.7 mm strip, and a thin 0.7 mm strip with a 0.2 mm stiff layer reaches only 6 percent of the ceiling (f=0.096). No experimental data were produced; the FEM verifies the algebra and the geometry, not the material behaviour.
lay_summary: We wrote a small computer model of a strip made of two glued layers, where one layer swells and the other does not, like a bimetal strip in a thermostat. The older formula says the strip can never curl tighter than a fixed limit, no matter how stiff or soft each layer is. Our model agrees with that formula to better than one part in a million for a strip that can curl freely. It also showed that a very wide sheet that is forced to curl in only one direction can curl up to about half as much again, which the simple formula misses. And it showed that wide strips lose some curl because bending in two directions at once stretches the middle, like trying to wrap paper round a ball. Finally, it warns that a very soft layer on a very stiff one only reaches the limit if the stiff layer is hair-thin, about the width of two printed layers, which is too thin for the printers to make reliably.

glossary.plain: a strip made of two bonded layers of different material.
how much more one layer wants to grow than the other, as a fraction of its length (0.01 means 1 percent).
how tightly a strip bends; one divided by the radius of the circle it follows.
how many times stiffer one layer is than the other.
how many times thicker one layer is than the other.
a computer method that cuts a part into many small pieces, solves each piece's push and pull, and adds them up.
a thin sheet free to thicken or thin out in the direction we do not draw, like a free strip.
the strip is held so it cannot change length in the hidden direction, like a very wide sheet.
how much a material gets thinner sideways when you stretch it; about 0.3 for hard plastic and near 0.5 for rubber.
a saddle shape (curls opposite ways in two directions) versus a bowl shape (curls the same way).
a plate theory that keeps the stretching caused by a strongly bent plate, which the simple linear theory leaves out.
a method that guesses a smooth family of shapes and picks the one with least stored energy.
the number that multiplies swelling strain divided by thickness to give the bend of a two-layer strip; its largest value is 1.5.
local disturbance near a free end that fades within about one thickness.

findings.claim: A 1-D force-and-moment balance solved by linear algebra (no closed form used) reproduces the project-record Timoshenko coefficient f(m,n) to rounding error over m=0.05..20 (81 log-spaced points) and n=1,2,5,10,50.
findings.evidence_quote: max |f_numeric - f_closed| over m in [0.05,20] (81 pts), n in [1, 2, 5, 10, 50]: 2.887e-15

findings.claim: On a fine grid of 400001 values of m, the maximum of f is 1.5 at m = n^-0.5 for n = 1, 2, 5, 10, 50; the 3/2 ceiling is reached to 2e-11 or better and modulus ratio drops out at the optimum.

2-D plane-stress FEM (9-node quads, free strip, L/h=40, 50 (m,n) points per case) reproduces Timoshenko f to 1.2e-7 relative error at worst; the worst point is n=10, m=0.05 (thin stiff layer, mesh and fit limited).
The largest FEM coefficient over the plane-stress grid is 1.50000 (ratio to the 3/2 ceiling 1.00000), reached at m=n^-0.5; FEM never exceeds the ceiling.
findings.evidence_quote: largest FEM coefficient = 1.50000 at n=50, m=0.14142  (ceiling 3/2 = 1.5; ratio 1.00000)

findings.claim: Mesh refinement (3 meshes, up to 10626 dofs) and strip length (L/h = 5 to 80) change the central-window curvature by at most 8.2e-4 relative to Timoshenko (worst: L/h=5, m=20, n=50); for L/h>=20 it is below 2e-6. Because the problem is a uniform-eigenstrain one, the quadratic elements represent the interior solution exactly.

A ruler-style measurement (end-to-middle sagitta, 8*delta/L^2) differs from the central curvature by an end effect that scales as (h/L)^2: 4.2 percent at L/h=10 and 17 percent at L/h=5 for the extreme case m=20, n=50; for the n=10 optimum it is 0.29 percent at L/h=10. A measured tip deflection on a short strip therefore needs this correction before comparing with the law. I did not determine the physical cause of the offset.

Plane strain (strip held from changing width, eps_z=0) with equal Poisson ratios multiplies the plane-stress coefficient by exactly 1+nu: FEM/Timoshenko ranged 1.29999938 to 1.30000007 for nu=0.30 and 1.48999813 to 1.49000606 for nu=0.49 over 50 (m,n) points; the ceiling becomes 1.95 (nu=0.30) or 2.235 (nu=0.49). The generalised formula (1+nu1)*f(m, n*(1-nu2^2)/(1-nu1^2)) matches the FEM to 4e-6 for all four cases including nu1=0.49, nu2=0.35.
findings.source: results/s02_output.txt and s02_sweep.csv; derivation: sigma_x = E/(1-nu^2)[eps_x - (1+nu) eps*] for eps_z=0, sigma_y=0 (own derivation, code in fem2d.f_plane_strain_generalised)
findings.evidence_quote: largest FEM coefficient = 2.23500 at n=1, m=1  (ceiling 3/2 = 1.5; ratio 1.49000)

findings.claim: With unequal Poisson ratios (nu1=0.49 swelling layer, nu2=0.35 passive) the plane-strain FEM coefficient is 1.291 to 1.675 times the plain Timoshenko value over the grid (min at n=50, m=20; max at n=1, m=0.05); the ceiling is still (1+nu1)*3/2 = 2.235, independent of n, and of nu2 (FEM 2.2321 to 2.2338 at the plain-Timoshenko optimum, which shifts slightly).
findings.source: results/s02_sweep.csv (case D_planestrain_nu0.49_0.35), analysis in this run

findings.claim: 3-D linear FEM (27-node hexahedra, L/h=20, widths w/h = 0.5 to 32) with equal Poisson ratios gives the curvature along the strip equal to Timoshenko to better than 1e-4 at every width and every (m,n) tested (1,1; 0.316,10; 0.2,10; 1,10; 0.05,10; 20,50). Width does not change the linear-regime curvature.
findings.value: largest equal-nu deviation 0.0000 (below 5e-5) at m=20, n=50, w/h=8
findings.evidence_quote: largest |kx/f_Tim - 1| with equal Poisson ratios = 0.0000 at m=20.0, n=50, w/h=8

findings.claim: With Poisson ratio mismatch (0.49 in the swelling layer, 0.35 in the passive layer, m=n^-0.5, n=10) the 3-D linear curvature is 0.17 to 0.32 percent below Timoshenko at all widths (0.99726 at w/h=8, 0.99734 at w/h=32; worst 0.99680 at w/h=1). Plate theory (classical laminate theory) gives 0.99731 for a wide plate, matching.

In the linear regime the free bilayer is synclastic across the width, not anticlastic: the cross-width curvature divided by the length curvature is +0.9992 to +1.0001 for w/h >= 4 (equal Poisson ratios), because swelling is an isotropic free strain rather than an applied moment (an applied moment would give -nu). For w/h <= 2 the quadratic fit across the section is not meaningful (values from -0.17 to +50 depending on case), so I make no claim there.

Classical laminate theory for a free plate with equal Poisson ratios gives a spherical shape with curvature exactly f*d_eps/h in both directions (1.000000 of Timoshenko), so Timoshenko's strip value is also the thin-plate small-deflection value.
findings.evidence_quote: linear CLT free-plate curvature / (f d_eps): 1.000000 (x), 1.000000 (y)  [sphere, equals Timoshenko for equal Poisson ratios]

findings.claim: Large-deflection (von Karman, Ritz, polynomial degree 4) model, optimum n=10 bilayer, L/h=40, d_eps=1 percent: curvature along the strip relative to Timoshenko f*d_eps/h is 0.999 at w/h=4 (lam=0.24), 0.986 at w/h=8 (lam=0.96), 0.942 at w/h=12 (lam=2.16), 0.866 at w/h=16 (lam=3.84), 0.730 at w/h=24 (lam=8.64); lam = f*d_eps*(w/h)^2. Cross-width curvature falls faster (0.970, 0.873, 0.712, 0.364). The length curvature stays within 2 percent of Timoshenko up to lam of about 1, i.e. up to w of about h/sqrt(f*d_eps).

Sensitivity of the Ritz result to the trial space: going from degree 2 to 4 changes the length curvature by at most 0.017 (0.713 to 0.730 at lam=8.64) but the cross-width curvature by up to 0.11 (0.470 to 0.364), so the length-curvature numbers are good to about 2 points and the cross-width numbers to about 10 points.

I did not reach the cylinder regime. At the widest case allowed by the model's validity (w/h=32, w/L=0.8, lam=15.4) the lowest-energy shape is nearly a cylinder (cross-width curvature 0.05 of f*d_eps/h) but its length curvature is 0.847 of Timoshenko, not the (1+nu) amplification expected for a fully constrained wide sheet. The sphere-to-cylinder change is a gradual crossover here (L is not equal to w, so the bifurcation is imperfect); I cannot say where a sharp switch would be. The von Karman theory is limited to moderate rotation (I kept f*d_eps*L/(2h) <= 0.3 rad), which prevents reaching larger lam.

Extreme modulus contrast: 2-D FEM with 8 elements per layer reproduces Timoshenko for n up to 2000 at m = n^-0.5 (1.50007 vs 1.50000 at n=2000) and within 1.9e-4 at off-optimum m (worst: n=2000, m=0.00745).

Design consequence (inputs are project-record estimates, not measurements): a soft layer with a secant modulus of about 5.8 MPa (Flexible 80A V2 estimate from spec-formlabs-materials.json) over Rigid 10K at about 10.5 GPa gives n=5.52e-4 (1/n=1810) and an optimum soft:stiff thickness ratio m*=42.5. With the stiff layer at the 0.2 mm Form 4 minimum supported wall, the optimum total thickness is 8.71 mm; a 0.7 mm total strip (m=2.5) has f=0.0957 (6.4 percent of the ceiling).
findings.evidence_quote: stiff layer 0.2 mm -> optimal total thickness h* = ts*(1+m*) = 8.71 mm

findings.claim: Bend radius for that pair using the project record's 1-day linear swelling strain 0.99 percent (derived from +3 percent volume): at a 0.05 mm stiff layer and 2.0 mm soft layer (h=2.05 mm, f=1.4999) R is 138 mm; at 0.1 mm / 1.0 mm (f=1.125) R is 99 mm; at 0.2 mm / 2.0 mm (f=1.125) R is 198 mm. One-week strain 2.28 percent gives 60, 43, 86 mm. These use the plane-stress law and assume the strain is uniform through the active layer, which diffusion makes untrue for days.
findings.source: results/s07_output.txt; strain inputs from D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/bm-resin-water-uptake-data.json (peer file, not re-verified)

findings.claim: CONFIRMS spec-bilayer-physics.json: the loss from equal thickness is 33.6 percent at n=10 and 75 percent at n=50, and the closed-form optimum f=3/2 at m=n^-0.5 is correct (that file derived it itself and found no published statement of it; I verified it numerically and by FEM, not from a source).
findings.evidence_quote: curvature loss relative to 3/2 at equal thickness m=1: n=1: 0.0%, n=2: 3.0%, n=5: 16.7%, n=10: 33.6%, n=50: 75.0%

findings.claim: REFINES spec-bilayer-physics.json item (d), 'A plate cannot hold bilayer curvature in two directions once width exceeds about sqrt(h/kappa)'. In my large-deflection model the loss is gradual and small at that width (w=sqrt(h/kappa) corresponds to lam=1: length curvature 1.4 percent low, cross-width 3 percent low, still bowl-shaped); two-way curvature is lost by 27 percent (length) and 64 percent (width) only at about 3 times that width (lam=8.6). The scale sqrt(h/kappa) = h/sqrt(1.5 d_eps) is right as an onset, 'cannot hold' is too strong, and the earlier file's missing numerical prefactor is now: 1.4 percent loss at w = 1.0*sqrt(h/kappa), 6 percent at 1.5, 13 percent at 2.0 (n=10 optimum, d_eps 1 percent). Caveat: polynomial trial space, one aspect ratio family (L/h=40).

QUALIFIES the project-record statement that the curvature ceiling is exactly 3/2: it is the ceiling for a strip free to deform in its hidden direction (plane stress, and in 3-D linear theory at any width). For a sheet held to a cylinder (plane strain) the ceiling is (1+nu1)*3/2 (1.95 for nu=0.30, 2.235 for nu=0.49), still independent of n. This is consistent with the earlier file's '(1+nu) times beam curvature' and with a published mean curvature 3/4 of the natural one only if nu=0.5 (cylinder mean curvature = kappa_x/2 = 0.75 kappa_0); I did not read the cited paper and I did not reach the cylinder regime in the plate model, so the (1+nu) factor is verified in 2-D plane strain only.
findings.evidence_quote: largest FEM coefficient = 1.95000 at n=50, m=0.14142  (ceiling 3/2 = 1.5; ratio 1.30000)

key_claims.claim: The Timoshenko coefficient and its 3/2 ceiling at m=n^-0.5 are reproduced by independent numerics: 1-D balance to 2.9e-15, 2-D plane-stress FEM to 1.2e-7 over n=1..50, m=0.05..20, and to 5e-5 at the optimum up to n=2000.
The ceiling is 3/2 only for a free strip. A sheet held to a cylinder (plane strain) reaches (1+nu1)*3/2: 1.95 at nu=0.30 and 2.235 at nu=0.49; modulus ratio still drops out.
key_claims.evidence_quote: largest FEM coefficient = 2.23500 at n=1, m=1  (ceiling 3/2 = 1.5; ratio 1.49000)

key_claims.claim: In the 3-D linear model the curvature along the strip is independent of width (equal Poisson ratios: under 1e-4 deviation; mismatched 0.49/0.35: at most 0.32 percent low) and the cross-width curvature is synclastic, not anticlastic.

The practical width limit is geometric: in the large-deflection model the length curvature is 1.4 percent below Timoshenko at w = h/sqrt(f*d_eps) and 13 percent below at twice that width (optimum n=10 bilayer, L/h=40), so strips narrower than about h/sqrt(f*d_eps) behave as the 1-D law.

recommendations: Quote the ceiling as 3/2 for a free strip and state the plane-strain version (1+nu1)*3/2 wherever a wide sheet or a clamped/constrained layout is meant; the Lean theorem is about the beam coefficient and does not cover this, so a second Lean statement (E' = E/(1-nu^2), d_eps' = (1+nu)d_eps) would make the plane-strain claim machine-checked too.

For the proof-of-concept strips keep w <= h/sqrt(f*d_eps) (for h=0.8 mm, f*d_eps=1.5 percent: w <= 6.5 mm) if the 1-D law is to be tested cleanly; wider test strips will read 5 to 15 percent low and that is the geometry, not a failure of the law.
When comparing a measured tip or sagitta deflection with the law, use strips with L/h >= 40, or correct for the (h/L)^2 end offset measured in s03, and report the width ratio w/h with it.

Do not plan on the 3/2 optimum for a soft-on-rigid Formlabs pair: the stiffness contrast near 1800:1 puts the optimum stiff layer at about 2 percent of thickness (0.2 mm stiff layer needs an 8.7 mm strip, where water diffusion is too slow). Choose pairs with n of about 10 to 50 (stiff layer 14 to 32 percent of thickness at the optimum) or accept f of about 0.4 to 1.1.

Measure, do not estimate, the inputs the model needs: a wet/dry length change for one printed Formlabs resin, and its Poisson ratio and modulus wet and dry; the FEM already shows that a Poisson-ratio mismatch of 0.14 (0.49 versus 0.35) moves the plane-strain curvature by -13 to +12 percent relative to the equal-Poisson-ratio case (ratio 1.29 to 1.67 against 1.49).

could_not_find: Experimental data for any printed Formlabs bilayer, or any measured wet/dry strain or Poisson ratio for a Formlabs resin: none produced here and none found by earlier agents; the simulation therefore checks the law's mathematics and geometry, not the real material. The soft-pair design numbers use project-record estimates (5.8 MPa secant modulus, 0.99 and 2.28 percent strain) that I did not re-verify.

The cylinder regime of the wide-plate nonlinear problem: the von Karman Ritz model is only valid to moderate rotation (I kept f*d_eps*L/(2h) <= 0.3 rad) and never reached the (1+nu) cylinder amplification; (1+nu) is verified only in 2-D plane strain. A geometrically exact 3-D nonlinear FEM (for example FEniCSx) was not attempted. I did not try FEniCSx at all.

A sharp critical width for the sphere-to-cylinder switch: in this model with L different from w the transition is a smooth crossover and the cross-width curvature depends on the trial-space size by up to 0.11.
Physical cause of the (h/L)^2 end offset in the end-to-middle sagitta measurement (s03); I only report its size.

Not modelled: moisture diffusion (strain is taken as uniform through the swelling layer), viscoelasticity and creep, material nonlinearity at the 5 to 70 percent strains of hydrogels and elastomers, layer-wise anisotropy of printed parts, bond-line compliance, and plasticisation (modulus change on wetting).
I read none of the cited papers (DOI and title checks only); I could not check what Timoshenko 1925, Hyer 1981 or Pezzulla 2016 print for the coefficients I compare with.

Headroom note: when I started, free C: was about 453 MB (under the 1 GB rule) and free D: 9.8 GB. I ran only small computations (under 2 GB RAM, one core) and installed numpy, scipy and scikit-fem (about 190 MB download, 192 MB installed) with pip cache disabled and both the target and TMP on D:. Free C: read 414 MB afterwards; I cannot tell whether any of that drop came from my work.
